roman/nymph-with-conch-sestino.text: A shell and the folds gathered at the hips give this figure a direct connection to water. The statue decorated the cold-bathing room of Roman Sestino, where it occupied a wall niche; its fragments were recovered from a pool. The scan project identifies its design with Roman adaptations of Venus types used around fountains and baths. That setting gives the shell a practical architectural context, rather than identifying the figure as a particular named nymph.

europe/nymph-echo-lemoyne-louvre.text: Echo reclines against a rocky support, her drapery following the extended line of the marble figure. The 1822 Salon catalogue explained the turn of her body through the story of Narcissus: hearing his lament over his reflection, she turns toward the man who has rejected her. Lemoyne made the sculpture in Rome for the Duke of Berwick and Alba and signed it in 1821. The Salon text describes it as a companion to a Narcissus looking into water.

europe/triton-and-nymph-after-tilgner-mi.text: This is the Mirbach Palace's 1981 bronze cast after Viktor Tilgner's model of 1875–77, a composition shaped by his encounter with Italian sculpture. Bratislava City Gallery identifies the action as Triton abducting a sea nymph. The entwined figures and strongly directed movement give that carrying-off a physical force, while the courtyard fountain's running water extends the marine subject into the surrounding space. Identifying the later cast preserves the work's history as a nineteenth-century design reintroduced into a twentieth-century setting.

europe/triton-and-naiad-fountain-haerdtl.text: Haerdtl's fountain is one of four sculptural centres distributed across Vienna's Maria-Theresien-Platz, and the Wien Museum's historical photograph identifies his group at the northwest of the square. The clustered human and marine bodies turn the fountain into a composition to be read around its centre, while water joins the modeled forms in the same setting. It belongs to the late nineteenth-century transformation of the space between Vienna's two imperial museums into an architectural and sculptural ensemble.

modern/vase-with-naiad-coulon-saintes.text: Produced at the Manufacture Nationale de Sèvres in 1902 after Jean Coulon's design, this stoneware bouquet holder lets a water-spirit figure determine the vessel's structure. The naiad bends around a fish whose open mouth provides the vase's opening, joining bodily motion to the object's use. Yellow, brown and greenish marbling runs across the intertwined forms, making the ceramic surface part of the aquatic effect. The Saintes museum's description emphasizes the sculptural possibilities of stoneware, which Coulon treats with the ambition of statuary on a domestic scale.

modern/vase-masks-nymphs-satyrs-injalber.text: Injalbert showed this monumental marble vase at the Salon of the Société nationale des beaux-arts in 1905, extending decorative sculpture to the scale of a substantial gallery object. Nymphs, satyrs and masks emerge in high relief, so the vessel's surface becomes an inhabited composition rather than a smooth container. The contrast between rounded bodies, folds of drapery and the dense marble ground gives the carving its animated play of projection and shadow. The museum's designation as high relief makes the border between vase and sculpture central to reading it.

roman/seated-nymph-brussels.text: This surviving marble figure belongs to the long afterlife of Greek sculptural designs in Roman collections. The scanner identifies it as a Roman replica after a Greek composition from Asia Minor. One leg crosses the other above deeply folded drapery, while the remaining hand rests against the rocky seat. The missing head and forearm make the sculpture’s fragmentary survival immediately visible, alongside the contrast between the smooth torso and the more heavily worked fabric.

roman/satyr-and-nymph-townley-british-mu.text: This Roman marble group combines an archaeological survival with the history of restoration and collecting. Found near Tivoli, it entered the British Museum with Charles Townley’s collection in 1805. The nymph braces against the satyr as their arms and bent legs form a tightly connected composition. The museum’s exhibition label identifies her action as resistance to an attempted rape. Later restoration of the nymph’s head shapes the expression now visible, making the group’s reception inseparable from its changing physical appearance.

baroque/thetis-caspar-gras-ferdinandeum-.text: Caspar Gras modeled this seated bronze sea deity for the ensemble commissioned by Archduke Leopold V. Her turning head, bent knee and the curving creature held close to her body give a compact figure movement from several viewpoints. The fountain’s sculptures had a long history of separate display before being brought together in 1893. The original bronzes are now preserved in the Ferdinandeum, while copies occupy the outdoor fountain.

baroque/apollo-and-daphne-852483.text: Soldani condensed the myth of Daphne’s transformation into a small terracotta group made in Florence around 1700. Her raised hands become branches as bark climbs her legs, while Apollo’s reaching body and the surrounding figures concentrate the action around the tree. Cleveland identifies Bernini’s earlier marble as the source of the composition. Modeling the subject in clay allowed Soldani to organize a complex, fleeting event through projecting limbs, swirling drapery and sharply changing directions.

europe/galatea-le-lorrain-nga.text: Le Lorrain’s marble Galatea brings the sea nymph into a carefully balanced seated composition. A shell in one hand and marine creatures below the rock establish the watery setting, while gathered cloth and the turned head carry movement across the figure. Its documented history begins at the Académie Royale in Paris in 1701. The sculpture later passed through French collections before entering the National Gallery of Art with the Samuel H. Kress Collection in 1952.

europe/amphitrite-coysevox-louvre.text: Coysevox carved Amphitrite for the water gardens at Marly, where mythological figures formed part of Louis XIV’s sculptural landscape. The sea goddess sits amid broad folds of drapery, with a raised cloth framing the turning head and marine forms at the base. Commissioned with Neptune and two river groups, the marble belonged to an ensemble planned around flowing water. Its later journey through public gardens, Brest and wartime storage ended with transfer to the Louvre in 1966.

europe/amphitrite-prou-louvre.text: Jacques Prou made this marble Amphitrite for a carp basin in the gardens of Marly. The figure rests on a broad marine support, with the turned head and gathered legs extending the composition across its low base. Commissioned in 1704 and paid for in 1705 and 1706, the sculpture was later moved to Marly’s Amphitrite fountain. Its changing placement shows how a single mythological figure could be adapted within a royal garden’s evolving arrangement of basins and cascades.

europe/apollo-daphne-stanetti-belvedere.text: The outstretched arms of Daphne and Apollo’s lyre make this garden group legible across the space around it. Drapery and the tree support connect their opposing movements, while the carved pedestal extends the classical setting below. The group is dated around 1720 and traditionally attributed to Giovanni Stanetti. A conservation organization records its move from the Belvedere orangery to the lower park around 1850 and its restoration in 1997, showing how the sculpture’s setting has changed over time.

europe/eurydice-macdonald-ngi.text: Lawrence MacDonald presents Eurydice drying herself after bathing, before the fatal event that begins the familiar story of Orpheus’s journey to the underworld. The inclined head, bent knee and cloth gathered at the hip turn the figure into a study of balance and carved fabric. Commissioned by the sixth Viscount Powerscourt in 1837, the marble was designed for viewing in the round. After years outside at Powerscourt, conservation at the National Gallery of Ireland recovered its bright marble surface.

americas/naiad-tragic-mask-calder-pafa.text: Calder joins a water nymph with a theatrical mask in this compact sculptural arrangement of about 1920. The figure bends forward, drawing one arm down beside the plinth while the knees and shoulders carry movement back into the seated body. PAFA identifies the material as plaster painted green and white, with surviving evidence of gold leaf. Those deliberately varied surfaces distinguish the figure, mask and support and preserve the work’s history as a modeled and painted object.

contemporary/nymphs-of-the-spring-schwai.text: Schwaiger gives the water-nymph subject a concentrated sculptural form through four closely fitted figures. Bent knees, lifted arms and overlapping bodies create an interlocking mass, while the marble surface carries the marks of an outdoor life in Kurpark Oberlaa. The group, titled Quellnymphen, dates from 1974. Its compact arrangement makes the spaces between the figures as important as their outlines, adapting a classical subject to a twentieth-century public park.

modern/daphne-sellier-bayssan-e4aa9d.text: Emmanuel Sellier uses the change from figure to tree to organize this 2021 treatment of Daphne. Her lowered head and folded arms gather the upper body into a narrow shape, while the trunk spreads into a rougher support below. The identified material, Kuros doré marble, allows smooth and irregular passages to coexist within one stone. The contrast of worked surfaces makes the transformation readable as a gradual passage between human form and the branching structure of a tree. The location of this scanned example remains unverified: the commission record names Bayssan, while the capture publisher names Toulouse.

renaissance/nymph-and-satyr-met-64-101-1.text: This small Renaissance group brings a nymph and satyr together in twisting poses, contained within a compact, weighty silhouette. In a study published by the Met, Rolf Bagemihl connected that combination to early sixteenth-century drawings that reworked classical figures. The piece is dated 1506 and has long been associated with the Volterran sculptor Zaccaria Zacchi. Its title does not identify a particular pursuit or transformation, so the encounter should remain unnamed rather than being assigned a story from Ovid.

renaissance/nymph-of-fontainebleau-celli.text: Designed for a gateway, this broad bronze relief joins a nymph with a stag and other animals into one architectural field. The forest imagery matters as much as the central figure: the Louvre records dogs, a hind and fawn, a boar, fruit and an amphora among its subjects. Francis I commissioned it for Fontainebleau, but the unfinished relief was later installed above the entrance at Anet. Casting it in eight parts made this large, detailed surface possible.

baroque/apollo-and-daphne-bernini-borghe.text: Daphne’s raised arms become branches while her feet take root: Bernini carved the instant in which she escapes Apollo’s pursuit by changing into a laurel. Apollo’s lifted foot and reaching hand sustain the forward movement as the marble shifts from skin to bark and leaves. The story comes from Ovid, where Daphne asks her father, the river god Peneus, to change her form. The group was originally arranged against a wall so visitors discovered the transformation as they approached.

europe/bather-or-nymph-at-bath-nga.text: The figure inclines her head and points one foot forward as though testing water. Her other hand reaches behind to a tree stump, balancing the forward movement; the cloth held at her thigh and the round base keep the composition compact. The NGA identifies this marble as an eighteenth-century French carving after a model dated 1757, with Falconet listed as a related artist. Its bathing action suggests a nymph, but the title leaves that identification open.

europe/pan-pursuing-syrinx-godecharle-lo.text: Godecharle compresses Pan’s pursuit of Syrinx into a small terracotta group. The Louvre identifies fear, a spring and reeds among its subjects, linking the movement of the figures to Syrinx’s escape through transformation in Ovid’s story. The clay version probably served as a model for a much larger stone group, completed with variations in 1804. This earlier object preserves the scene at an intimate scale and should be distinguished from that later outdoor sculpture.

europe/nymph-and-satyr-huntington.text: A seated satyr holds grapes above a nymph who lies across his knees and turns her face upward. Pipes, a tambourine and a thyrsus place the pair within the world of Bacchic music and celebration, without identifying them as a named mythological couple. The dark bronze group rests on a contrasting blue-grey marble base. Once credited to Clodion, this particular sand-cast bronze is now catalogued by the Huntington as the work of an unknown French maker around 1850–1875.

europe/nymph-with-scorpion-bartolini-lou.text: Bartolini developed this marble from a plaster model of about 1835. The marble was acquired for the château of Haroué around 1843 and exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1845. The nymph's hand returns to the foot pierced by a scorpion, while her lips part only slightly. These small interruptions of repose make pain legible without breaking the figure's flowing contour, and the finely worked marble gives that restrained gesture a convincing bodily presence.

americas/clytie-rinehart-met.text: Rinehart translated Ovid's story into the controlled language of American Neoclassical marble sculpture. The Met identifies Clytie as the water nymph abandoned by Apollo and transformed after her sustained vigil toward the sun. A drooping sunflower in her right hand carries the narrative, while live sunflowers climb the tree stump beside her. That stump has a practical role as well: it braces the marble figure, joining a sculptor's structural solution to the story's transformation.

europe/nymph-of-loch-awe-pomeroy-tate.text: Pomeroy's small recumbent figure belongs to the late Victorian revival of ambitious sculpture acquired through the Chantrey Bequest, which brought this work to Tate in 1897. Tate connects it with Scottish folklore, sleep and drowning. The figure's low horizontal pose gives the subject a quiet, suspended stillness, while the pale marble body and separate onyx base place the modeled figure against a material that can suggest the water of its title.
